lessons.title: Classroom Action Research: Process and Ethics

lines: Action research is done by teachers in their own classrooms to improve teaching and learning. Kemmis and McTaggart's cycle: plan, act, observe, reflect, then plan again.
Steps: identify a problem, gather baseline data, plan an intervention, carry it out, collect and analyze data, reflect, and share results (for example in a School LAC).

Ethics: informed consent (from parents for minors), confidentiality, voluntary participation with the right to withdraw, and honesty. Fabricating data and plagiarism are serious misconduct. Triangulation uses several data sources to confirm a finding. Minors also give their own assent. Member checking asks participants to confirm the researcher's summary of their views. Changing a few words of a source while keeping its sentences (patchwriting) is plagiarism even with a citation. Falsification is changing or leaving out real data; fabrication is inventing data that were never collected.
A teacher leaves out two low posttest scores so that her intervention looks more effective. What is this?
Changing or omitting real data is falsification. Inventing data that were never collected is fabrication. Both are serious research misconduct.
Action research is a cycle, not a one-time study: plan, act, observe, reflect, then plan again with what was learned.
Writing a research question too broad to act on, such as "Is the K to 12 program effective?" Action research asks about one's own class and an intervention one can try.

Research questions should be specific and focused on one's own learners. Variables: the independent variable is what the teacher changes (the intervention); the dependent variable is the outcome measured (such as scores). A hypothesis is a testable prediction. The null hypothesis states no significant difference or relationship; the alternative hypothesis states that there is one.

Approaches: quantitative research uses numbers and statistics (scores, ratings); qualitative research uses words and meanings (interviews, reflections), often analyzed by grouping answers into themes (thematic analysis); mixed methods combines both. A sample is the subset of the population actually studied: random sampling gives everyone an equal chance; purposive sampling picks participants with specific characteristics. A pilot test tries out an instrument on a small group first. Stratified sampling picks randomly from each subgroup (such as each grade) in proportion to its size; cluster sampling picks whole groups, such as entire sections. Comparing intact sections without random assignment is quasi-experimental. A single Likert-type item gives ordinal data.

Designs: pretest-posttest, quasi-experimental (intact classes), descriptive, correlational, and qualitative designs such as case studies. Tools: questionnaires (often with Likert scales), interviews, observation and tests; pilot-test tools first and have experts check content validity.
A teacher studies whether sending text reminders to parents increases the number of homework assignments learners complete. What is the dependent variable?
The outcome being measured is homework completion; the text reminders are the independent variable.
sections.answer: The number of homework assignments completed

lines: To find the dependent variable, ask "What is being measured to see if it changed?"
Calling a comparison of two existing sections a true experiment. Without random assignment of learners to groups, the design is quasi-experimental.

lessons.subject: Language and Linguistics
lessons.title: Sounds and Words: Phonetics, Phonology and Morphology

lines: Branches of linguistics: phonetics (how speech sounds are made), phonology (how sounds pattern in one language), morphology (word structure), syntax (how words form phrases and sentences), semantics (meaning) and pragmatics (meaning in context).

Consonants are described by voicing, place and manner. /p/, /b/ and /m/ are bilabial (both lips); the "th" in "think" is a voiceless dental fricative. The schwa /ə/ is the unstressed mid-central vowel, as in the first syllable of "about".

Phonemes are sounds that change meaning; minimal pairs prove it ("ship" and "sheep"). Allophones are variants of one phoneme that do not change meaning, such as the aspirated /p/ in "pin" and the unaspirated /p/ in "spin". Allomorphs are different pronunciations of one morpheme: the plural is /ɪz/ after sibilants (buses), /s/ after other voiceless sounds (cats) and /z/ after other voiced sounds (dogs).
Stress can change a word: REcord (noun) and reCORD (verb). Many two-syllable verbs are stressed on the second syllable (beGIN, reLAX).
How many morphemes are in "unhappiness"?
A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning. "Happy" is a free morpheme; "un-" and "-ness" are bound morphemes.

Inflectional suffixes add grammar without changing the word class (-s, -ed, -ing, -er in "taller"). Derivational affixes make new words, often changing the class (teach to teacher, happy to happiness).

Word formation: blending (breakfast + lunch = brunch), clipping (examination to exam), compounding (classroom), acronyms (NASA), borrowing (kindergarten), coinage (a new word, often from a brand) and conversion (using "email" as a verb). Back-formation removes a supposed affix to make a new word (editor to edit, television to televise).

English has only eight inflectional morphemes: plural -s, possessive 's, third-person -s, past -ed, past participle -en, progressive -ing, comparative -er and superlative -est. Every other affix is derivational. (Linguists often call possessive 's a clitic, since it attaches to a whole noun phrase: "the king of England's crown".)
Counting "-er" in "teacher" as inflectional. There it is derivational (it makes a noun from a verb); only the "-er" of comparison, as in "taller", is inflectional.

lessons.subject: Language and Linguistics
lessons.title: Sentences and Meaning: Syntax, Semantics and Pragmatics

lines: Syntax: a noun phrase is built around a noun ("the tall teacher"); a transitive verb takes a direct object ("She wrote a letter"), while an intransitive verb does not ("She smiled"). A relative (adjective) clause modifies a noun ("the book that I borrowed"). Structural ambiguity comes from two possible structures ("I saw the man with the telescope"); lexical ambiguity comes from one word with two meanings.
Sentence types by structure: simple (one independent clause), compound (two or more independent clauses), complex (one independent clause and at least one dependent clause), compound-complex (both).
"Although it rained, the program continued." What kind of sentence is this?
"Although it rained" is a dependent clause; "the program continued" is independent. One of each makes a complex sentence.
The subjunctive mood expresses wishes and situations contrary to fact: "If I were you, I would apologize." "I suggest that he be on time."

Semantics: synonyms, antonyms, homonyms (same form, unrelated meanings: the "bank" of a river and a "bank" for money), and hyponymy ("rose" is a hyponym of "flower"; "flower" is the hypernym). Denotation is the dictionary meaning; connotation is the feeling attached.

Pragmatics studies meaning in context. "Can you pass the salt?" is a request, not a question about ability (an indirect speech act). A performative utterance does what it says ("I now pronounce you husband and wife"). Deixis covers words like "here", "now" and "you", whose meaning depends on who speaks, where and when. A presupposition is assumed background ("Ana stopped smoking" assumes she smoked). Grice's maxims of conversation are quantity (enough information), quality (truth), relation (relevance) and manner (clarity); flouting one on purpose creates an implied meaning. Austin separated the locutionary act (the words said), the illocutionary act (what the speaker does by saying them, such as requesting) and the perlocutionary act (the effect on the listener).
Semantics asks "What do the words mean?"; pragmatics asks "What does the speaker mean here?"
Calling every sentence with "and" compound. "She and I sang" is simple: it has one clause with a compound subject.

Chomsky proposed an inborn Language Acquisition Device and a Universal Grammar shared by all languages. Lenneberg's Critical Period Hypothesis holds that language is acquired most easily before puberty.

Krashen's theory of second language acquisition: acquisition (natural) differs from learning (conscious rules); the monitor edits output; grammar is acquired in a natural order; comprehensible input a little above the current level (i + 1) drives acquisition; and a high affective filter (anxiety, low confidence) blocks input.
Selinker's interlanguage is a learner's developing system, with its own rules, between the first language and the target language. Errors that stop changing are fossilized.
A speaker says, "Let's go na, we're late." What is this called?
Moving between two languages within one conversation is code-switching. "Taglish" is a common Philippine example.

Sociolinguistics studies language in society. Diglossia: two varieties with separate functions (one formal, one everyday). Varieties include dialects (regional), sociolects (social group), register (formality), jargon (a profession's terms) and slang.

Kachru's World Englishes: the Inner Circle (native, such as the US and UK), the Outer Circle (English as an official second language from colonial history, such as the Philippines, India and Singapore) and the Expanding Circle (English as a foreign language, such as Japan and China).

Policy: the 1987 Constitution names Filipino as the national language, with Filipino and English as official languages. The 1987 Bilingual Education Policy (DECS Order No. 52, s. 1987), building on a 1974 policy, used both as media of instruction. Later laws changed the rules, such as RA 10533 (K to 12, which added mother tongue-based instruction in the early grades) and RA 12027 (2024), which discontinued the mother tongue as the main medium of instruction in Kindergarten to Grade 3. The Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino (RA 7104) develops and promotes Filipino and the other Philippine languages.
Philippine English is a recognized variety of English, not a collection of mistakes.
Placing the Philippines in the Expanding Circle. English has official status here, so it is Outer Circle.

lessons.subject: Literature
lessons.title: Philippine Literature: Folk Traditions and Writing in English

lines: Folk literature: epics such as Biag ni Lam-ang (Ilocano), the Hudhud (Ifugao, chanted at harvests and funerals and recognized by UNESCO), Hinilawod (Panay) and Darangen (Maranao). In Tagalog mythology, Bathala is the supreme god and creator.
Literature in English began under American rule. "Dead Stars" (1925) by Paz Marquez-Benitez is often called the first modern Filipino short story in English.

Key writers: Jose Garcia Villa ("Doveglion"; the comma poems; "Footnote to Youth"), Nick Joaquin ("May Day Eve", "A Portrait of the Artist as Filipino"), Manuel E. Arguilla ("How My Brother Leon Brought Home a Wife", set in Ilocos), N. V. M. Gonzalez ("The Bread of Salt"), Carlos Bulosan ("America Is in the Heart"), Edith L. Tiempo ("Bonsai"; co-founder of the Silliman University National Writers Workshop) and F. Sionil José (the five-novel Rosales Saga). During the Japanese occupation (1942–1945), English was suppressed and writing in Tagalog flourished. The balagtasan, a debate in verse led by a lakandiwa, began in 1924; the older duplo was a verse game held at wakes.
Who wrote "Footnote to Youth", in which Dodong marries young and later sees his son repeat the same path?
Villa wrote the story in the 1930s, before turning almost entirely to poetry.
Link each writer to one keyword: Villa (commas), Joaquin (old Manila and the past), Arguilla (Ilocos countryside), Bulosan (migrant workers), Tiempo (Silliman), Sionil José (Rosales).
Assigning the Hudhud to the Ilocanos. Biag ni Lam-ang is Ilocano; the Hudhud is Ifugao.

Asia: the Epic of Gilgamesh (Mesopotamia, among the oldest known works), the Ramayana (Rama rescues Sita from Ravana) and the Mahabharata (India), Tagore's Gitanjali (Tagore was the first Asian Nobel laureate in literature, 1913), the Analects of Confucius (China), The Tale of Genji by Murasaki Shikibu and the haiku of Matsuo Bashō (Japan), the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam (Persia) and One Thousand and One Nights, told by Scheherazade. India's Panchatantra teaches wise conduct through animal fables; Japan's Noh drama uses masks and slow, stylized movement, while Kabuki is livelier and uses makeup.
Africa: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (an Igbo community under colonial rule) and Wole Soyinka of Nigeria, the first African writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1986).
Which poet wrote the haiku about an old pond and a frog jumping in?
Bashō is the best-known master of the haiku, a Japanese form traditionally of 5-7-5 syllables.

Mythology: Greek gods include Zeus (sky, king of the gods), Poseidon (sea) and Hades (underworld); Theseus killed the Minotaur in the labyrinth. Roman names differ (Zeus is Jupiter, Poseidon is Neptune). Norse mythology has Odin and Thor, the god of thunder.
Group works by country: India (Ramayana, Mahabharata, Gitanjali), Japan (Genji, haiku), China (Analects), Persia (Rubaiyat), Nigeria (Achebe, Soyinka).
Mixing Greek and Roman names in one answer. Poseidon and Neptune are the same god in two mythologies.

lessons.subject: Literature
lessons.title: English and American Literature, Forms and Elements

lines: English literature: Chaucer (The Canterbury Tales), Shakespeare (Hamlet, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet), Milton (Paradise Lost), Jane Austen (Pride and Prejudice). Romanticism (Wordsworth, Coleridge) stressed emotion, nature and imagination. Metaphysical poets such as John Donne used conceits, long surprising comparisons (two lovers as the legs of a compass). Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress is an allegory, in which characters stand for ideas.

American literature: Thoreau (Walden), Robert Frost ("The Road Not Taken"), Hemingway (The Old Man and the Sea), Shirley Jackson ("The Lottery"). Transcendentalists (Emerson, Thoreau) trusted intuition, self-reliance and nature.
A sonnet has 14 lines, traditionally in iambic pentameter. The Shakespearean sonnet has three quatrains and a closing rhyming couplet; the Petrarchan sonnet has an octave and a sestet.

Plot: exposition, rising action, climax (highest tension), falling action, resolution. Point of view: first person ("I"), third-person limited or omniscient. A theme is a general insight stated as a full idea ("Pride can blind people to love"), not a single-word topic. Irony: verbal (saying the opposite of what one means), situational (the opposite of what is expected happens) and dramatic (the audience knows what a character does not). Metonymy names something associated with the thing meant ("Malacañang announced"); synecdoche uses a part for the whole ("all hands on deck").
A novel follows a character growing from youth to maturity. What is this kind of novel called?
The coming-of-age novel is common in adolescent literature.

Children's literature includes fables (animal characters with a moral, such as "The Tortoise and the Hare") and legends (how something came to be, such as the legend of the pineapple). Contemporary forms include flash fiction (very short stories) and digital literature shared online, as on Wattpad.
A fable teaches a moral with animals; a legend explains an origin; a myth involves gods and the supernatural.
Calling the climax the end of the story. The climax is the turning point of highest tension; the resolution comes after it.

Methods: Grammar-Translation (translation, rules, vocabulary lists), Direct Method (target language only), Audio-Lingual (behaviorist drills, pattern practice, memorized dialogues), Total Physical Response (learners respond to commands with movement), Silent Way (the teacher mostly silent, with colored rods and charts), Suggestopedia (relaxation and music to lower anxiety) and Community Language Learning (Curran: the teacher acts as a counselor; learners say what they want in their first language, the teacher gives it in the target language, and learners repeat it, in a supportive group).

Communicative Language Teaching aims at communicative competence through meaningful communication. Task-Based Language Teaching organizes lessons around real tasks, such as planning a trip. Information-gap activities make partners exchange missing information. Presentation–Practice–Production (PPP) moves from teacher explanation to controlled practice to free use. Canale and Swain's communicative competence has four parts: grammatical, sociolinguistic (appropriate to the situation), discourse and strategic. Willis's task-based framework runs pre-task, task cycle (task, planning, report), then language focus.
A teacher uses only English in class, teaches new words with pictures and actions, and never translates. Which method is this?
The Direct Method teaches through the target language alone, linking words directly to meaning. Grammar-Translation, by contrast, relies on translation.
Match the clue to the method: drills (Audio-Lingual), commands with movement (TPR), rods (Silent Way), music and relaxation (Suggestopedia), translation (Grammar-Translation).
Calling every pair activity "communicative". Reading a scripted dialogue aloud is not communication; a communicative task needs a real exchange of meaning.

lessons.subject: Teaching English
lessons.title: Teaching the Macro Skills, Grammar and Vocabulary

lines: Macro skills: listening, speaking, reading and writing; the K to 12 curriculum adds viewing. Listening can be intensive (for detail or specific information) or extensive (longer listening for enjoyment). Speaking activities build accuracy or fluency; role play builds communicative competence in realistic situations. Corder separated errors (gaps in knowledge, not self-correctable) from mistakes (slips). Feedback types include recasts, explicit correction, elicitation, metalinguistic clues and repetition of the error with rising intonation. Top-down listening uses prediction and background knowledge; bottom-up listening focuses on sounds and words.

Grammar is best taught in context through meaningful texts and tasks. Vocabulary grows through context clues, word parts and repeated meaningful use. Beck's Tier 2 words (academic words used across subjects, such as "analyze") deserve the most direct teaching. A corpus with concordance lines lets learners discover how words are really used.
A learner says, "He go to school every day." The teacher replies, "Oh, he goes to school every day?" What kind of correction is this?
A recast repeats the learner's idea in correct form without stopping the conversation. Explicit correction states the error directly; elicitation prompts the learner to fix it.
Intensive listening is for details and specific information; extensive listening is for overall understanding and enjoyment.
Treating fluency activities as a time to correct every error. Constant interruption works against fluency; note errors and address them later.

Bottom-up processing builds meaning from letters, sounds and words; top-down processing uses background knowledge (schema) and prediction; interactive models combine both. Phonics teaches letter-sound relationships.

Strategies: skimming (for the general idea), scanning (for a specific detail), SQ3R (Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review). Levels of comprehension: literal (stated), inferential (implied), critical (evaluative) and creative or applied. Critical (evaluative) questions ask learners to judge and support a view.

The Phil-IRI places learners at the independent level (reads alone with ease), instructional level (reads with teacher support) or frustration level (too hard). A learner at frustration level needs easier texts and guided support. Remedial instruction reteaches the specific skills an assessment shows are weak, using new approaches and smaller steps, rather than repeating the same lesson. Repeated reading builds fluency.

Assessment: the cloze test deletes every nth word; miscue analysis studies oral reading errors (substitutions, omissions, insertions). Achievement tests cover a course; proficiency tests (such as IELTS) measure general ability; diagnostic tests find specific weaknesses; placement tests sort learners into levels. Integrative tests (cloze, dictation) use many skills at once; discrete-point tests check one item at a time. Washback is a test's effect on teaching. In a running record, the self-correction rate is (errors + self-corrections) ÷ self-corrections. Scorers agree more when they share one analytic rubric and calibrate on sample essays. Passages on one narrow topic (such as basketball) give an advantage to learners who know it, which weakens validity.
A teacher asks, "Why do you think the character lied?" The story does not say why. Which level of comprehension is this?
The answer must be read between the lines, which makes it inferential.
Graphic organizers: a Venn diagram to compare and contrast; a KWL chart (what I Know, Want to know, Learned); a story map for plot elements; a timeline for sequence.
Skimming is for the gist; scanning is for a specific item, such as a date or a name.
Giving a struggling reader harder texts to "challenge" them. At frustration level, comprehension breaks down; step down to the instructional level first.

lessons.subject: Teaching English
lessons.title: Teaching Writing, Journalism and Specialized Writing

lines: Process writing: prewriting, drafting, revising (improving content and organization), editing (fixing grammar and mechanics) and publishing. Peer editing gives learners feedback and trains them to evaluate writing. A thesis statement states an essay's main argument. In shared writing the teacher holds the pen and learners contribute ideas; in interactive writing learners share the pen.

Text types: narrative, descriptive, expository, persuasive and procedural (steps, such as a recipe for adobo). Creative writing: "show, don't tell"; sound devices such as alliteration (repeated initial consonants), assonance and onomatopoeia.

Campus journalism: RA 7079 (Campus Journalism Act of 1991). A straight news story follows the inverted pyramid, with the lead giving the most important facts, usually who, what, when, where, why and how. The editorial expresses the paper's official opinion; a feature story focuses on human interest. Copyreading corrects grammar, facts and style before publication. The inverted pyramid also lets editors cut from the end without losing key facts. A column is a recurring signed opinion piece; an editorial is usually unsigned and gives the paper's official stand.

Technical writing values clarity, accuracy and conciseness (user manuals, reports, instructions). A business letter has standard parts (heading, inside address, salutation, body, complimentary close and signature); its body carries the purpose and message, in a clear, concise and courteous tone. English for Specific Purposes teaches the English a group needs for its work, such as nursing.
A translator keeps the source text's word order and renders it word for word, even when it sounds unnatural. What kind of translation is this?
A good translation instead conveys the meaning and tone of the original naturally in the target language.
Revising changes ideas and organization; editing fixes sentences and mechanics. Revise first.
Starting a news story with background. The inverted pyramid puts the most important facts first.

lessons.subject: Teaching English
lessons.title: Teaching Literature, Criticism, Speech and Materials

lines: Approaches to literature: reader-response (learners share personal reactions and interpretations) and creative response (rewriting an ending, retelling from another character's view). Stylistics analyzes how word choice, sentence length and figures of speech create effects; discourse analysis studies longer stretches of language, such as turn-taking in conversation.

Criticism: formalism (the text alone: structure, imagery, language), historical-biographical (the author's life and times), Marxist (class and economic struggle), feminist (women and gender roles), psychoanalytic (hidden desires, using Freud), archetypal (recurring patterns such as the hero's journey). New Historicism reads a work alongside other texts of its time to study power and culture; deconstruction shows how a text undermines its own oppositions, so meaning stays unstable.
A class analyzes how a novel shows the conflict between rich landowners and poor farmers. Which approach is this?
A focus on social class and economic power marks Marxist criticism.

Speech and theatre: projection (speaking loudly enough without shouting), articulation, oral interpretation (reading literature aloud with expression), readers theater (reading a script expressively without costumes or full staging) and impromptu speaking (little or no preparation), as against extemporaneous (prepared, delivered from notes).

Materials: authentic materials (real menus, schedules, news articles) and contextualized or localized materials (a local news story about a recent flood). Technology such as class blogs gives learners a real audience and builds digital literacy. Descriptive research records and categorizes what happens, such as types of learners' errors.
Ask what the critic looks at: the text only (formalism), the author's life (biographical), class (Marxist), gender (feminist), the mind (psychoanalytic) or universal patterns (archetypal).
Confusing impromptu and extemporaneous speech. Impromptu has almost no preparation; extemporaneous is prepared but not memorized.

Ancient roots: the Egyptians left the Rhind Papyrus; the Babylonians used base 60, which survives in 60 minutes per hour and 360° in a circle. Indian mathematicians such as Brahmagupta treated zero as a number with its own rules, and the Hindu-Arabic numerals spread from India through the Islamic world.

Greece: Pythagoras (a² + b² = c²), Euclid (the "Father of Geometry"; the Elements built geometry from axioms), Archimedes (estimated π with polygons inside and outside a circle), Eratosthenes (the sieve for primes) and Hypatia of Alexandria, one of the earliest recorded women mathematicians.

Al-Khwarizmi's book "al-jabr" gave algebra its name; the word "algorithm" comes from his name. Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci) brought Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe in the Liber Abaci, which includes the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...

Modern era: Descartes (the Cartesian plane and analytic geometry), Pascal and Fermat (probability), Newton and Leibniz (calculus, developed independently in the 17th century), Euler (the notation f(x), e and i) and Gauss (the "Prince of Mathematicians").
As a schoolboy, Gauss is said to have quickly added the whole numbers from 1 to 100. What is the sum?
Pair the numbers: 1 + 100, 2 + 99, and so on give 50 pairs of 101, so the sum is 50 × 101 = 5,050.
Link each name to one idea: Euclid (Elements), Archimedes (π), al-Khwarizmi (algebra), Fibonacci (the sequence), Descartes (coordinates), Newton and Leibniz (calculus), Gauss (the 1-to-100 sum).
Crediting the Arabs with inventing zero. Zero as a number came from India; Arab and Persian scholars passed it on to Europe.

Inductive reasoning generalizes from examples ("2 + 4, 6 + 8 and 10 + 12 are all even, so the sum of two even numbers is even"); its conclusions are likely but not proven. Deductive reasoning applies general statements to reach certain conclusions. One counterexample is enough to disprove a general claim. For "if p, then q", the contrapositive (if not q, then not p) is always equivalent; the converse (if q, then p) and the inverse may be false. Proof methods: direct proof, proof by contradiction (assume the opposite and reach an impossibility, as for √2 being irrational) and mathematical induction (prove a base case, then that truth for k implies truth for k + 1). The negation of "if p, then q" is "p and not q".

A mathematical system has undefined terms (point, line, plane), definitions, axioms or postulates (accepted without proof) and theorems (proved). Lobachevsky, Bolyai and Riemann built non-Euclidean geometries by changing Euclid's parallel postulate. In spherical geometry a triangle's angles add up to more than 180°; in hyperbolic geometry, to less.
Which single number shows that "All prime numbers are odd" is false?
2 is prime and even. That one counterexample is enough.

Mathematical modeling represents a real situation with mathematics: identify the problem, make assumptions, build the model, solve it, interpret and check the results against the real situation, then refine the model. Repeated doubling or a fixed growth rate calls for an exponential model (P = P₀ · 2^(t/10) for doubling every 10 years), not a linear one.
A mathematical investigation is open-ended: learners explore a situation, look for patterns, make and test conjectures, and justify them, rather than finding one expected answer.
George Pólya's four steps: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back.
Examples suggest a rule (inductive); a proof establishes it (deductive).
Thinking that many examples prove a statement. No number of examples proves a general claim; only a proof does.

Quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0: solve by factoring or the quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells the roots: positive, two real; zero, one real; negative, no real roots. Sum of roots = −b/a; product = c/a.
Factoring patterns: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b); always take out the common factor first: 2x² − 18 = 2(x − 3)(x + 3).

Inequalities: multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the sign. |x − a| = k gives x − a = k or x − a = −k. To evaluate a function, substitute and follow the order of operations: if f(x) = x² + 1, then f(−3) = 9 + 1 = 10. Simplify a rational expression by factoring and canceling common factors: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = x + 2, for x ≠ 2. |x − a| < k means −k < x − a < k (a single interval); |x − a| > k gives two separate intervals.
Solve the system 2x + y = 9 and x − y = 3.
Adding the equations gives 3x = 12, so x = 4; then y = 9 − 2(4) = 1. Check: 4 − 1 = 3.
Check a solution by substituting it back into the original equation; this also catches sign errors.
Forgetting to flip the inequality sign: −2x > 6 gives x < −3, not x > −3.

Exponents: aᵐ · aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, a⁰ = 1, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. Exponential equations: write both sides with the same base (3^(x + 1) = 3⁴, so x = 3). Half-life decay halves the amount each period: after n half-lives, the amount is the original × (1/2)ⁿ.

Logarithms: log_b x = y means bʸ = x. log a + log b = log ab, so log 2 + log 5 = log 10 = 1. Simplify radicals by taking out perfect squares: √50 = 5√2. Check every solution of a log equation: a value that makes any logarithm's argument zero or negative is rejected.
Variation: direct y = kx (y grows with x), inverse y = k/x (y shrinks as x grows), joint y = kxz. Combined: y = kx/z² means y varies directly as x and inversely as the square of z.
Solve log₃ x = 4.
log₃ x = 4 means 3⁴ = x, so x = 81.
In a variation problem, find k first from the given pair, then use it for the new value.
Writing log a + log b as log (a + b). The rule is log a + log b = log ab.

Age problems: let one unknown stand for an age now; add the same number of years to every person for the future. Work problems: rates add, 1/a + 1/b = 1/t. Mixture problems: the amounts of the substance in the parts add up to the amount in the mixture (c₁V₁ + c₂V₂ = c × total volume). When only pure water is added, it adds none of the substance, so concentration × volume stays the same before and after.

Arithmetic sequence: aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d; sum Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. Geometric sequence: aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹; sum Sₙ = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1). A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence. An infinite geometric series with |r| < 1 has the sum S = a₁/(1 − r): 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + ... = 8/(1 − 1/2) = 16. A repeating decimal is an infinite geometric series: 0.272727... = 0.27 ÷ (1 − 0.01) = 27/99 = 3/11.
One pipe fills a tank in 4 hours and another in 12 hours. How long do they take together?
1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3 of the tank per hour, so together they take 3 hours.

Simple interest: I = Prt (principal × rate × time in years). Compound interest: A = P(1 + r)ⁿ for annual compounding; the interest earned is A − P. Compounded n times a year: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt); more frequent compounding gives slightly more.
Example: ₱10,000 at 5% compounded annually for 2 years gives 10,000 × 1.05² = ₱11,025, so the interest is ₱1,025, more than the ₱1,000 of simple interest.
Write the time in years before using I = Prt: 6 months is 0.5 year.
Answering a compound interest question with A when it asks for the interest. Subtract the principal.

Polygons with n sides: the interior angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°; each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360°/n; the number of diagonals is n(n − 3)/2. A hexagon has interior angles summing to 720° and 9 diagonals.

Areas: rectangle lw, triangle bh/2, trapezoid (b₁ + b₂)h/2, circle πr². Circumference is 2πr; an arc with central angle θ is (θ/360°) × 2πr. A square with side s has area s², perimeter 4s and diagonal s√2. The perpendicular from a circle's center bisects a chord, so the radius, half the chord and the distance from the center form a right triangle.
Volumes: prism and cylinder = base area × height (cylinder πr²h); pyramid and cone = (1/3) × base area × height (cone (1/3)πr²h); sphere (4/3)πr³. Surface areas: cube 6s², sphere 4πr².
Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c². Common triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and their multiples (9-12-15).
Similar figures with side ratio a : b have area ratio a² : b² and volume ratio a³ : b³. A sphere inside a cube of edge s has radius s/2.
What is each interior angle of a regular pentagon?
A cone holds one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height; remember the (1/3) for pointed solids.
Doubling the area when the sides double. Doubling every side multiplies the area by 4 and the volume by 8.

SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent. Special values: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, sin 45° = cos 45° = √2/2, tan 45° = 1, sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2.

Degrees to radians: multiply by π/180 (150° = 5π/6). Quadrants: I from 0° to 90°, II to 180°, III to 270°, IV to 360°. Signs follow "All Students Take Calculus": all positive in I, sine in II, tangent in III, cosine in IV. Use the reference angle: cos 120° = −cos 60° = −1/2.
Identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.
Any triangle: law of sines a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C; law of cosines c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
From a point 30 m from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation to the top is 30°. How tall is the tower?
The angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal; the angle of depression is measured down from it. Both are measured from the horizontal, never from the vertical.
Using the Pythagorean theorem on a triangle with no right angle. Use the law of cosines instead.

Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals (3 and −1/3). Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). Distance: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²); midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). A triangle's area from coordinates: ½ × base × height when one side lies on an axis, or ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)| in general.

Parabola in vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k has vertex (h, k) and axis of symmetry x = h; it opens upward if a > 0 and downward if a < 0. With p = 1/(4a), its focus is (h, k + p) and its directrix is y = k − p. Circle: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²; from the general form, complete the squares.
Find the center and radius of the circle x² + y² + 4x − 6y − 3 = 0.
Group and complete the squares: (x² + 4x + 4) + (y² − 6y + 9) = 3 + 4 + 9, so (x + 2)² + (y − 3)² = 16. The center is (−2, 3) and the radius is √16 = 4.
Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1: 3 × (−1/3) = −1.
Giving the slope of a perpendicular line as the reciprocal without changing its sign: for slope 3, it is −1/3, not 1/3.

Limits: if substitution gives 0/0, factor and cancel: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = x + 2, which approaches 4 as x approaches 2. At infinity, a rational function whose numerator and denominator have the same degree approaches the ratio of the leading coefficients.

Derivatives: d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹; d/dx sin x = cos x; d/dx cos x = −sin x; d/dx eˣ = eˣ, and by the chain rule d/dx e^(2x) = 2e^(2x). The derivative is the slope of the tangent line; a maximum or minimum can occur only at a critical point, where it is 0 or undefined. Check each one: if f′ changes from + to −, it is a maximum; from − to +, a minimum. (f(x) = x³ has f′(0) = 0 but no maximum or minimum there.) Product rule: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′. Optimization: write the quantity in one variable, set the derivative to 0 and check that it is a maximum or minimum.
Integrals: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C. A definite integral is F(b) − F(a). The area between two curves is the integral of (upper − lower).
Find the derivative of f(x) = 5x³ − 4x² + x − 9.
Apply the power rule term by term: 15x² − 8x + 1; the constant −9 has derivative 0.
Integration undoes differentiation: check an integral by differentiating your answer.
Forgetting "+ C" in an indefinite integral. Every antiderivative can differ by a constant.

The mean is the sum divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value after sorting (for an even number of values, the mean of the two middle ones); the mode is the most frequent value; the range is the highest value minus the lowest. Weighted mean = Σ(weight × value)/Σweights. Adding a constant to every score shifts the mean but leaves the range and standard deviation unchanged; multiplying every score by a number multiplies both the mean and the SD by it.

Probability = favorable outcomes/possible outcomes; P(not A) = 1 − P(A); independent events multiply. Permutations (order matters) nPr = n!/(n − r)!; divide by k! for each letter repeated k times. Combinations (order does not matter) nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). For "at least one", use 1 − P(none). Conditional probability: P(A given B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). Circular arrangements of n people: (n − 1)!. Choosing from two groups at once: multiply the combinations, C(4, 2) × C(6, 3). Exactly k successes in n fair coin tosses: C(n, k) ÷ 2ⁿ.
In how many distinct ways can the letters of LEVEL be arranged?
There are 5 letters, with L and E each appearing twice: 5!/(2! × 2!) = 120/4 = 30.
"Choose a committee" is a combination; "arrange", "rank" or "assign positions" is a permutation.
Using a permutation when order does not matter, such as when choosing a committee. That counts the same group many times over.

Logic: "p and q" is true only when both are true; "p or q" is false only when both are false; "if p then q" is false only when p is true and q is false. The contrapositive (if not q, then not p) is equivalent to the original. The negation of "All A are B" is "Some A are not B".
Sets: a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets; n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

Numbers: GCF × LCM = the product of two numbers. To test whether n is prime, try primes up to √n. Modular arithmetic works with remainders: 2³ = 8 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 7. Last digits of powers repeat in cycles (7, 9, 3, 1 for powers of 7), so divide the exponent by the cycle length.
If n(A) = 12, n(B) = 9 and n(A ∩ B) = 4, how many elements are in A ∪ B?
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) = 12 + 9 − 4 = 17. Subtracting the overlap avoids counting it twice.
To test whether 91 is prime, try only the primes up to √91 (about 9.5): 2, 3, 5 and 7. Since 91 = 7 × 13, it is not prime.
Writing the negation of "All teachers are patient" as "All teachers are not patient". One impatient teacher is enough: "Some teachers are not patient."

lessons.subject: Teaching Mathematics
lessons.title: Approaches and Strategies in Teaching Mathematics

lines: Concrete-pictorial-abstract (CPA) moves from objects to drawings to symbols, following Bruner's enactive, iconic and symbolic modes. Manipulatives: base-ten blocks, fraction strips, geoboards and algebra tiles (to model polynomial operations). Skemp separated instrumental understanding (knowing the rule) from relational understanding (knowing the rule and why it works). In a 5E lesson, Elaborate applies a concept to a new, harder situation.

Van Hiele levels of geometric thinking: visualization (shapes recognized by appearance), analysis (by properties), informal deduction (relationships among properties), formal deduction (proofs) and rigor. Showing one idea in multiple representations (a table, a graph and an equation of the same function) helps learners connect them and deepens understanding.

Problem solving: let learners struggle productively with a problem before showing a method. Pólya's steps end with "look back" (check if the answer is reasonable). Strategies: draw a diagram, make an organized list, look for a pattern, guess and check, work backward, solve a simpler problem.

Other practices: inquiry-based learning (learners investigate and build ideas), think-pair-share, heterogeneous grouping, learning stations for different needs, Bloom's mastery learning (reach a set level before moving on, with corrective help), number talks for mental computation, and the spiral K to 12 curriculum.
In Bruner's modes, learners who study fractions by shading parts of drawn circles are working in which mode?
Pictures and diagrams are iconic; objects are enactive; numerals and symbols are symbolic.

Technology: dynamic software such as GeoGebra lets learners change m and b in y = mx + b and watch the graph move; spreadsheets suit real data learners collect; calculators fit when the goal is exploring or understanding, not drilling computation. Journals and "why" questions build mathematical communication and higher-order thinking.
Motivate with real contexts: tiling a floor for area, sale prices for percent, a class budget for operations.
Skipping the concrete and pictorial stages for learners who are not ready. Symbols without meaning lead to memorized rules that are quickly forgotten.

lessons.subject: Teaching Mathematics
lessons.title: Misconceptions, Assessment and Research in Mathematics

lines: Common misconceptions: "multiplying always makes bigger" (0.5 × 8 = 4), "a longer decimal is bigger" (0.25 < 0.5, a place value misconception), "(a + b)² = a² + b²" (an area model of a square with side a + b shows the missing 2ab), and "the same perimeter means the same area". Confront them with counterexamples and models, not just the rule.

Error analysis (finding and explaining the mistake in a worked solution) builds conceptual understanding. When an error keeps coming back, follow up diagnostically (a few targeted items or a short interview to find the faulty idea), reteach that idea with a different model or representation, then check again. Reduce anxiety by treating mistakes as part of learning and lowering time pressure.

Assessment: exit slips are formative; an analytic rubric scores understanding, strategy and answer separately; matching tests mainly check recall. A performance task applies mathematics to a realistic job, such as planning a class party within a ₱2,000 budget. An aligned item asks learners to do exactly what the objective says, for example solve a real-life percent problem.

Research: action research (a teacher improves own practice), quasi-experimental (intact sections, no random assignment), simple random sampling (everyone has an equal chance), the null hypothesis (no significant difference or relationship). The paired t-test compares two sets of scores from the same learners (pretest and posttest). A Type I error is concluding there is an effect when there is none; a Type II error is missing a real effect.
Which test compares the mean scores of two separate groups, such as a game-based class and a traditional class?
For three or more groups use ANOVA; for a relationship between two measures use Pearson's r; for counts in categories use chi-square.
Levels of measurement: nominal (names or categories), ordinal (ranks, such as 1st, 2nd, 3rd), interval (equal intervals, no true zero, such as °C) and ratio (a true zero, such as height or weight).
Ask what the study compares: two means (t-test), three or more means (ANOVA), a relationship (Pearson r), frequencies (chi-square).
Concluding the new strategy "caused" higher scores from a correlation alone. Correlation shows a relationship, not cause.
